newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn says BSE calf may have been born in Britain.
newsitem.headline: Bonn says BSE calf may have been born in Britain.

text.p: A Galloway calf at the centre of a German scare over mad cow disease may have been illegally imported from Britain and not born in Germany as was first thought, an Agriculture Ministry spokesman said on Friday.
The case caused alarm in Germany when it was confirmed this week, as it appeared the calf was the first born locally to die of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) or mad cow disease.

"The regional authorities are investigating where the calf came from...and looking into the possibility it came from Britain," the spokesman said of the calf that died on a farm near the western town of Hoexter in December.

German officials ordered on Wednesday the slaughter 5,200 British and Swiss cattle on farms across Germany next week to calm consumer fears. Britain and Switzerland have recorded the largest number of BSE cases.
The officials also put the 14,000 calves of the British and Swiss cows under observation until tests established whether the Galloway calf was born in Germany to a British cow, as was first thought.
The spokesman said the 5,200 imported cattle would still be slaughtered, but not their 14,000 calves, if the calf proved to have been born outside Germany and illegally imported into the country.
He said many documents relating to the calf from a farm in eastern Germany, where it was previously kept, were missing.
Authorities were investigating the possibility that Galloway cattle had been illegally imported into eastern Germany from Britain via the Czech Republic, he said.
The calf was originally thought to have been born to an apparently healthy British mother cow, which was slaughtered in the Netherlands last year.
If experts proved she was in fact the mother, it would add weight to fears that BSE can be maternally transferred and proposals to kill the 14,000 calves would definitely go ahead.
The Association of Cattle Breeders in the northern states of Schleswig-Holstein and Hamburg protested against the planned cull and vowed to take legal action against it.
It said its members' cattle posed no danger to consumers and the 347 cattle imported from Britain to the two states were already under observation for any signs of BSE.
